title: Orca Encounters
text:
Orcas are nasty fish that enjoy munching on people!
Nope! There are several things that are wrong with that picture. Orcas are cetaceans related to dolphins that live in all of the world oceans. They are higly intelligent predators that hunt in coordinated family pods using very elaborate strategies. Their varied diet includes fish, sharks, smaller marine mammals (e.g. see lions), and even whales. But not humans!

title: Palm Trees of the World
text:
Palm trees can be tall! Or very short…
Palm trees are quite variable in height ranging from 0 to 170 meters. Palm tress can be grouped by Tribes (a taxonomic rank between family and genus). Members of some tribes are taller than trees in other tribes. Calameae and Lepidocaryeae are two tribes with particularly tall trees.

title: Dear Abby
text:
Where do you get intimate advice?
Seeking advice from friends is not always easy. Not everyone is a good confidant and sometimes our secrets are too embarrasing or too delicate to reveal outloud. For centuries, the truthwordy confidants of people with power were individuals bound by a vow of secrecy, priest for example. With the development of the printed press and later the radio, people found a chance to anonimously shared their stories and ask for advice.
In Spain the most famous radio advice show, El Consultorio de Elena Francis, run continuously from 1947 to 1984. For nearly four decades, millions of Spanish women tuned in or wrote letters to Señora Francis seeking guidance on personal issues, relationship struggles, family drama, and domestic problems. Interestingly, the show became the moral watchdog of the Franco regime. The responses broadcasted reflected the conservative, patriarchal, and Catholic values endorsed by the Francoist regime. Advice frequently encouraged women to endure infidelity, domestic hardship, or mistreatment, emphasizing patience, devotion, and submission to preserve the family structure.
The Señora Francis of the USA is Dear Abby, a column that has been runnng countiously since 1956 and has been sindycated in more than 1,200 newspapers. The letters sent to Dear Abby have been compilated by The Pudding, an award-winning digital publication that creates visual essays and interactive data visualizations to explain culturally debated topics and complex ideas.
In the The Putting article, 30 Years of American Anxietis, authors Ilia Blinderman, Caitlyn Ralph, and Russell Samora (with illustrations by Thoka Maer) identify the most debated topics by Dear Abby readers: sex, religion, and LGBTQ issues. The articule include =s some of the letters that are worth reading.
Here, I do my own analysis of 20034 Dear Abby letters from 1985 to 2017 from an archive which can be found in the The Pudding Github site.
I am using word clouds to reveal some of the most prevalent topics of the letters. No filters were applied to the top cloud including all the available letters (1985-2017), so words like abby appear, as expected, with high frequency. For the clouds for specific years, I have removed a list of words including Abby, dear, advice, letter, and letters.

title: The Pudding
text:
Word clould
The code below willl generate a word cloud using ggplot2. The code was generate by Google Gemini.
The code below also generates a word cloud and it was also provided by AI (Google Gemini)

library(wordcloud2)

# Input requires a 2-column data frame (word, freq)
df <- data.frame(
  word = c("R", "Data", "Science", "Visualization", "Ggplot", "Code", "Analysis"),
  freq = c(50, 40, 35, 30, 25, 20, 15)
)

# Render interactive HTML cloud
wordcloud2(data = df, size = 0.7, shape = 'circle', color = 'random-dark')

title: DS002R - HW 3 - Wrangling
text:
Introduction
In this assignment, we dive into using data wrangling to summarize datasets quantitatively and to format datasets so that they can be visualized.
Back to the Midwest… this time, wrangling.
In this part you will revisit and build on some of your findings from HW 2, where you explored the midwest data frame. Remember that the data frame is bundled with the ggplot2 package and is automatically loaded when you load the tidyverse package. As a refresher, the data contains demographic characteristics of counties in the Midwest region of the United States. You can read documentation for the data set, including variable definitions by typing ?midwest in the Console or searching for midwest in the Help pane.






Note



The data in the midwest data frame are from the 2000 census, so the information you compute below is likely slightly different from the values today.



Question 1
Calculate the number of counties in each state and display your results in descending order of number of counties. Which state has the highest number of counties, and how many? Which state has the lowest number, and how many?






Note



Commands Without Chaining by_state <- group_by(midwest, state) count_by_state <- summarize(by_state, count = n()) count_by_state_sorted <- arrange(count_by_state, desc(count)) view(count_by_state_sorted)


With Chaining

  midwest |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarize(count = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(count)) 

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  state count
  <chr> <int>
1 IL      102
2 IN       92
3 OH       88
4 MI       83
5 WI       72


ANSWER: Illinois has the the highest number of counties (102) and Wisconsin has the lowest (72)


Question 2
Within a state, two counties can’t have the same name, but across states county names can be shared. A friend says “Look, there is a county called XYZ in EVERY state in this dataset!” In a single pipeline, discover all counties that could fill in the value of XYZ. Your output should be a data frame with two columns: county and the number of times they appear in the data.






Tip



You will want to use the filter() function in your answer, which requires a logical condition to describe what you want to filter for. For example filter(x > 2) means filter for values of x greater than 2, filter(y <= 3) means filter for values of y less than or equal to 3.



operator
definition




<
less than


<=
less than or equal to


>
greater than


>=
greater than or equal to


==
exactly equal to


!=

x & y
x AND y


x | y
x OR y


is.na(x)
test if x is NA


!is.na(x)
test if x is not NA


x %in% y
test if x is in y


!(x %in% y)
test if x is not in y


!x
not x



The table above is a summary of logical operators and how to articulate them in R.



 midwest |>
  group_by(county) |>
  summarize(count = n()) |>
  filter(count >= 2) |>
  arrange(desc(count))

# A tibble: 70 × 2
   county     count
   <chr>      <int>
 1 CRAWFORD       5
 2 JACKSON        5
 3 MONROE         5
 4 ADAMS          4
 5 BROWN          4
 6 CLARK          4
 7 CLINTON        4

10 WASHINGTON     4

Question 3
Consider the following box plot of population densities where you can see that some counties have extreme values.









Identify the counties described in each part:

The counties with a population density higher than 25,000. Your code must use the filter() function.


midwest |>
filter(popdensity >= 25000) |>
select(county,state,popdensity,poptotal,area) |>
arrange(desc(popdensity))

# A tibble: 9 × 5
  county    state popdensity poptotal  area
  <chr>     <chr>      <dbl>    <int> <dbl>
1 COOK      IL        88018.  5105067 0.058
2 MILWAUKEE WI        63952.   959275 0.015
3 WAYNE     MI        60334.  2111687 0.035
4 CUYAHOGA  OH        54313.  1412140 0.026
5 DU PAGE   IL        39083.   781666 0.02 
6 MARION    IN        34659.   797159 0.023
7 HAMILTON  OH        34649.   866228 0.025
8 FRANKLIN  OH        28278.   961437 0.034
9 MACOMB    MI        25621.   717400 0.028



The county with the highest population density. Your code must use the max() function.


midwest |>
filter (popdensity == max(popdensity)) |>
select(county,state,popdensity,poptotal,area) 

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  county state popdensity poptotal  area
  <chr>  <chr>      <dbl>    <int> <dbl>
1 COOK   IL        88018.  5105067 0.058








Note



Answer using a single data wrangling pipeline for each part. Your response should be a data frame with five columns: county name, state name, population density, total population, and area, in order. If your response has multiple rows, the data frame should be arranged in descending order of population density.




Question 4
Let’s say that you want to describe the distribution of population densities. The following is one acceptable description (in words) that touches on shape, center, and spread of this distribution. Create a plot that fits the description, and use data verbs to calculate the values that should go into the blanks. [You might want to look up the quantile() function by typing ?quantile into the Console.]

The distribution of population density of counties is unimodal and extremely right-skewed. A typical Midwestern county has population density of ____ people per unit area. The middle 50% of the counties have population densities between ___ to ___ people per unit area.







Tip



Think about which measures of center and spread are appropriate for skewed distributions. That is, there is a right answer for the choice of functions you use to calculate the center and spread.



ggplot(midwest, aes(x = popdensity)) +
geom_histogram(binwidth = 1000) +
labs(
x = "Population density",
y = "Number of Counties",
title = "Population density of midwesten counties",
subtitle = "Binwidth = 1000"
)














Note



Remember that a right-skewed or right-tailed distribution leans to the left and is said to have positive skew.


Another option no so pretty.

ggplot(midwest, aes(x = popdensity, y = after_stat(density))) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1000, fill = "lightblue", color = "green") +
  geom_density(color = "red", linewidth = 0.6) +
  labs(
    x = "Population Density",
    y = "Density",
    title = "Population Density of Midwestern Counties",
    subtitle = "Histogram with overlaid density curve"
  )









midwest |>
  # select(popdensity) |>
  pull(popdensity) |>
  quantile(probs = seq(0,1,0.25), na.rm = FALSE)

        0%        25%        50%        75%       100% 
   85.0500   622.4074  1156.2083  2330.0000 88018.3966 


ANSWER: The distribution of population density of counties is unimodal and extremely right-skewed. A typical Midwestern county has population density of 1156 people per unit area. The middle 50% of the counties have population densities between 622 to 2330 people per unit area.


Question 5
Recall the visualization from HW 2 that showed the proportion of urban counties in each state.

midwest <- midwest |>
  mutate(metro = if_else(inmetro == 1, "Yes", "No"))

ggplot(midwest, aes(x = state, fill = metro)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "Do some states have more urban counties than others?",
    x = "State",
    y = "Proportion in metro area",
    fill = "In metro area?"
  )








In a single data pipeline, calculate the proportion of counties in a metro area for each state (that is, the turquoise number from the plot above).

midwest |>
  mutate(metro = if_else(inmetro == 1, "Yes", "No")) |>
  group_by(state)  |>
  summarize(
    yes_count = sum(metro == "Yes"),
    no_count  = sum(metro == "No"),
    ratio  = yes_count / (yes_count + no_count)) |>
    arrange(desc(ratio))

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  state yes_count no_count ratio
  <chr>     <int>    <int> <dbl>
1 OH           40       48 0.455
2 IN           37       55 0.402
3 MI           25       58 0.301
4 WI           20       52 0.278
5 IL           28       74 0.275

Question 7

In a single pipeline (with multiple data verbs), calculate the total population for each state and save the resulting data frame as state_population and display it in descending order of total population.


 midwest |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarize(state_population = sum(poptotal)) |>
  arrange(desc(state_population))

Then, in a separate pipeline, calculate the proportion of the total population in each state (e.g., find the percent of people living in WI out of all the people in the midwest) and, once again, display the results in descending order of proportion of population.


 midwest |>
  mutate(midwest_pop = sum(poptotal)) |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarize(perc_mdw_pop = sum(poptotal*100/midwest_pop))|>

Tip



In answering parts (a) and (b), you’ll create two new variables, one for total population and other for proportion of total proportion. Make sure to give them “reasonable” names – short but evocative.



Which Midwestern state is most populous and what percent of the Midwest population lives there? Which is the least populous and what percent lives there?

ANSWER: The most populous is Illinois with 27.2% of the pop[ulation of midwestern states. Wisconsin is the least populated with 11.6%of the toal.


Question 8
Calculate the average percentage below poverty for each state and save the resulting data frame as state_poverty with the columns state and mean_percbelowpoverty.
Then, in a new pipeline, display the state_poverty data frame in ascending order of mean_percbelowpoverty. Which state has the lowest average percentage below poverty across its counties? Which state has the highest average percentage below poverty across its counties?

 state_poverty <- midwest |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarize(mean_percbelowpoverty = mean(percbelowpoverty))
state_poverty

  state mean_percbelowpoverty

ANSWER: The Midwest state with the lowest average percentage below poverty across its counties is Indiana (~10%) and the state with the highest average below poverty is Michigan (~14%).

title: Dear Abby
text:
Abby in 2015









The word husband since the most frequent word that emerges from the letter published in though several decades. Is that because women are the main writters of Abby? In order to investigate this a bit further I have selected letters that include the words “my husband” and “my wife” hoping that this indentifies the writer. This is obviously not a perfect strategy. The word clouds below come from those letters. Assuming that the writers are talking about their partners, what are the word freqencies telling us about the letters? Are the themes different? Have they changed through time?
